steps.scene: You arrive at a crash. Someone is lying still in the road, and traffic is still moving past.

options.text: Run straight to the casualty
Check it's safe to approach
Drag them onto the pavement

question.explanation: If you get hurt too, there are two casualties and no helper. Make the scene safe before you go in.

steps.title: DR ABC
steps.prompt: Put the first checks on an unconscious casualty in order.

items.text: Response — try to get a response

steps.explanation: Then C: if they're not breathing normally, start chest compressions.

steps.title: Leave them where they are
steps.body: Don't move a casualty unless they're in further danger, such as from traffic or fire. They may have injuries you can't see.

question.prompt: A casualty is unconscious but breathing. When should you move them?

options.text: Straight away, into a more comfortable position
As soon as someone else can help lift
Only if they're in further danger

question.explanation: Moving someone with a neck or back injury can make it much worse.

steps.title: A rider's helmet
steps.body: Leave an injured motorcyclist's helmet on unless it's essential to remove it — for example, to keep their airway open.

question.prompt: A motorcyclist is injured after a crash. When should their helmet be removed?

options.text: Only when it's essential
Straight away, to help them breathe
Once they've been moved to the kerb

question.explanation: Pulling off a helmet can move the head and neck. Leave it to the paramedics unless there's no other way.

a.label: Adult CPR
a.body: Two hands on the centre of the chest. Press 5–6 cm, about twice a second.

b.label: Child CPR
b.body: One hand may be enough. Press 4–5 cm, at the same rate.

question.prompt: How far should you press down when giving CPR to an adult?

options.text: Just 1–2 cm, so you don't hurt them
5 to 6 centimetres
As far as you possibly can

question.explanation: Compressions must be hard and fast to keep blood moving. Don't stop unless they start breathing or help takes over.

steps.title: Public defibrillators
steps.body: Anyone can use a public defibrillator (AED). It talks you through every step, and the 999 operator can tell you where the nearest one is.

question.prompt: Who can use a public access defibrillator (AED)?

options.text: Only trained first aiders
Anyone
Only the emergency services

question.explanation: An AED won't shock someone who doesn't need it. If someone else is there, send them for one while you do CPR.

steps.scene: A pedestrian has a deep cut to their leg and is bleeding heavily. The leg isn't broken and there's nothing in the wound.

options.text: Let it bleed freely first to clean the wound
Give them a drink to replace lost fluid
Apply firm pressure over the wound

question.explanation: Firm pressure slows the bleeding. Protect yourself from their blood if you can, and keep the pressure on until help arrives.

steps.wrongBelief: Someone in shock after a crash should be given a hot, sweet drink.

question.prompt: A driver seems to be in shock after a crash. How can you help?

options.text: Reassure them confidently and keep them warm
Give them a hot, sweet drink
Walk them around to calm them down

question.explanation: Shock can be serious and isn't always obvious. Stay with them and watch for changes until help arrives.

steps.repairNote: Keep them warm and reassure them. Don't give them anything to eat or drink.
